task: wikipedia:Bicycle_chain (rev <2020-01-01)
text:
A bicycle chain is a roller chain that transfers power from the pedals to the drive-wheel of a bicycle, thus propelling it. Most bicycle chains are made from plain carbon or alloy steel, but some are nickel-plated to prevent rust, or simply for aesthetics.

Obsolete chain designs previously used on bicycles included the block chain, the skip-link chain, and the Simpson lever chain. The first chains were of a simple, bushing-less design. These had inherent reliability problems and a bit more friction (and mechanical efficiency losses) than modern chains. With these limitations in mind, the Nevoigt brothers, of the German Diamant Bicycle Company, designed the roller chain in 1898, which uses bushings, and it is the prevalent chain today. Whether it be single rear cog (for example coaster-brake single-speed or with an internal-gears hub), fixed-gear (such as track bikes and modern urban "fixies") or multi-speeds with derailleurs, all modern chains in use today are of the "roller chain" design. Although it is still possible to order lower cost "bushing-less" chains from China today, with generally lower manufacturing costs across the board, bushing-less chains are generally considered undesirable and not prevalent.

Before the safety bicycle, bicycles did not have chains and the pedals were typically attached directly to the drive-wheel, thus limiting top speed by the diameter of the wheel and resulting in designs with front wheels as large as possible. Various linkage mechanisms were invented to raise the effective gear ratio, but with limited success. Using chain drive allowed the mechanical advantage between the drive and driven sprockets to determine the maximum speed, thereby enabling manufacturers to reduce the size of the driving wheel for safety. It also allowed for the development of variable gearing, allowing cyclists to adjust their gearing on the fly, to terrain or road inclination and their strength, obtaining an efficient and workable cadence at various speeds.

A bicycle chain can be very energy efficient: one study reported efficiencies as high as 98.6%. The study, performed in a clean laboratory environment, found that efficiency was not greatly affected by the state of lubrication. A larger sprocket will give a more efficient drive because it moves the point of pressure farther away from the axle, placing less stress on the bearings, thus reducing friction in the inner wheel. Higher chain tension was found to be more efficient: "This is actually not in the direction you'd expect, based simply on friction".

task: wikipedia:Disc_brake (rev <2020-01-01)
text:
A disc brake is a type of brake that uses the calipers to squeeze pairs of pads against a disc or "rotor" to create friction. This action slows the rotation of a shaft, such as a vehicle axle, either to reduce its rotational speed or to hold it stationary. The energy of motion is converted into waste heat which must be dispersed.

Development of disc-type brakes began in England in the 1890s. In 1902, the Lanchester Motor Company designed brakes that looked and operated in a similar way to a modern disc-brake system even though the disc was thin and a cable activated the brake pad. Other designs were not practical or widely available in cars for another 60 years. Successful application began in airplanes before World War II, and even the German Tiger tank was fitted with discs in 1942. After the war, technological progress began to arrive in the 1950s, leading to a critical demonstration of superiority at the 1953 24 Hours of Le Mans race, which required braking from high speeds several times per lap. The Jaguar racing team won, using disc brake equipped cars, with much of the credit being given to the brakes' superior performance over rivals equipped with drum brakes. Mass production began with the 1955 Citroën DS.

Compared to drum brakes, disc brakes offer better stopping performance because the disc is more readily cooled.  As a consequence discs are less prone to the brake fade caused when brake components overheat.  Disc brakes also recover more quickly from immersion (wet brakes are less effective than dry ones).

Most drum brake designs have at least one leading shoe, which gives a servo-effect. By contrast, a disc brake has no self-servo effect and its braking force is always proportional to the pressure placed on the brake pad by the braking system via any brake servo, braking pedal, or lever.  This tends to give the driver better "feel" and helps to avoid impending lockup. Drums are also prone to "bell mouthing" and trap worn lining material within the assembly, both causes of various braking problems.

The disc is usually made of cast iron, but may in some cases be made of composites such as reinforced carbon–carbon or ceramic matrix composites. This is connected to the wheel and/or the axle. To slow down the wheel, friction material in the form of brake pads, mounted on the brake caliper, is forced mechanically, hydraulically, pneumatically, or electromagnetically against both sides of the disc. Friction causes the disc and attached wheel to slow or stop.

text:
Water for baths, sinks and basins can be provided by separate hot and cold taps; this arrangement is common in older installations, particularly in public washrooms/lavatories and utility rooms/laundries. In kitchens and bathrooms, mixer taps are commonly used. In this case, hot and cold water from the two valves is mixed before reaching the outlet, allowing the water to emerge at any temperature between that of the hot and cold water supplies. Mixer taps were invented by Thomas Campbell of Saint John, New Brunswick, and patented in 1880.
 uses a center handle to control both water flow and temperature (increased by clockwise rotation).  Below it is a lever controlling a diverter, sending flow to the tap when positioned to the left, the shower to the right.]]
For baths and showers, mixer taps frequently incorporate some sort of pressure balancing feature so that the hot/cold mixture ratio will not be affected by transient changes in the pressure of one or other of the supplies. This helps avoid scalding or uncomfortable chilling as other water loads occur (such as the flushing of a toilet).
Rather than two separate valves, mixer taps frequently use a single, more complex, valve controlled by a single handle (single handle mixer). The handle moves up and down to control the amount of water flow and from side to side to control the temperature of the water. Especially for baths and showers, the latest designs are thermostatic mixing valves that do this using a built-in thermostat, and can be mechanical or electronic. There are also taps with color LEDs to show the temperature of the water.

If separate taps are fitted, it may not be immediately clear which tap is hot and which is cold. The hot tap generally has a red indicator while the cold tap generally has a blue or green indicator. In the United States, the taps are frequently also labeled with an "H" or "C". In countries with Romance languages, the letters "C" for hot and "F" for cold are used (from French "chaud"/Italian "caldo"/Spanish "caliente" (hot) and French "froid"/Italian "freddo"/Spanish "frio" (cold)). This can create confusion for English-speaking visitors. Mixer taps may have a red-blue stripe or arrows indicating which side will give hot and which cold.

task: wikipedia:Jump_start_(vehicle) (rev <2020-01-01)
text:
A jump start, also called a boost, is a method of starting a vehicle with a discharged or dead battery. A temporary connection is made to the battery of another vehicle, or to some other external power source. The external supply of electricity recharges the disabled vehicle's battery and provides some of the power needed to crank the engine. Once the vehicle has been started, its  normal charging system will recharge, so the auxiliary source can be removed. If the vehicle charging system is functional, normal operation of the vehicle will restore the charge of the battery.

Motorists may carry jumper cables in case of accidental discharge of the vehicle battery (for example, by headlights or ignition switch left on while the engine is not running). Safe procedures for connecting and disconnecting cables are given in the vehicle manual.

Jumper cables, also known as booster cables or jump leads, are a pair of insulated wires of sufficient capacity with alligator clips at each end to interconnect the disabled equipment/vehicle with an auxiliary source, such as another vehicle or equipment with the same system voltage or to another battery. The alligator clips may be covered in insulation to prevent inadvertent shorting. Clips may be made of copper or steel. Alligator clips are generally marked by black (−) and red (+) to indicate the polarity.

Operation of a lead-acid battery may, in case of overcharge, produce flammable hydrogen gas by electrolysis of water inside the battery. Jump start procedures are usually found in the vehicle owner's manual. The recommended sequence of connections is intended to reduce the chance of accidentally shorting the good battery or igniting hydrogen gas. Owner's manuals will show the preferred locations for connection of jumper cables; for example, some vehicles have the battery mounted under a seat, or may have a jumper terminal in the engine compartment.

If the dead battery is physically damaged, has a low electrolyte level, is decayed or frozen, a jump start will not repair the battery. A vehicle with a frozen battery should not be jump started, as the battery may explode.

A hand-portable battery, equipped with attached cables and charger, can be used similarly to another vehicle's battery.
A self-contained jump box contains a battery and connects directly to the battery of the engine that needs a boost. Portable boosters may automatically sense the battery's polarity prior to sending power to the vehicle, eliminating the damage that can result from reversing the connection. There are various portable jump starters that are multi-functional and can be used to charge other electronic devices as well.

task: wikipedia:Heat_pump (rev <2020-01-01)
text:
A heat pump is a device that transfers heat energy from a source of heat to what is called a thermal reservoir. Heat pumps move thermal energy in the opposite direction of spontaneous heat transfer, by absorbing heat from a cold space and releasing it to a warmer one. A heat pump uses external power to accomplish the work of transferring energy from the heat source to the heat sink.
The most common design of a heat pump involves four main components – a condenser, an expansion valve, an evaporator and a compressor. The heat transfer medium circulated through these components is called refrigerant.

While air conditioners and freezers are familiar examples of heat pumps, the term "heat pump" is more general and applies to many heating, ventilating, and air conditioning (HVAC) devices used for space heating or space cooling. Heat pumps usually can be used either in heating mode or cooling mode, as required by the user. When a heat pump is used for heating, it employs the same basic refrigeration-type cycle used by an air conditioner or a refrigerator, but in the opposite direction – releasing heat into the conditioned space rather than the surrounding environment. In this use, heat pumps generally draw heat from the cooler external air or from the ground.

In the heating mode, heat pumps are significantly more energy efficient than simple electrical resistance heaters. However, the typical cost of installing a heat pump is higher than that of a resistance heater (see below).

When discussing heat pump efficiencies, the following terms are commonly used: coefficient of performance (COP), seasonal coefficient of performance (SCOP) and seasonal performance factor (SPF). The higher the number, the more efficient a heat pump is, the less energy it consumes, and the more cost-effective it is to operate. There are several factors that will affect the efficiency of a heat pump such auxiliary equipment, technology, size and control system, but also temperature and humidity conditions: the efficiency drops when the temperature difference increase or when freezing can occur.

Heat energy naturally transfers from warmer places to colder spaces. However, a heat pump can reverse this process, by absorbing heat from a cold space and releasing it to a warmer one. This process requires some amount of external energy, such as electricity. In heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) systems, the term heat pump usually refers to vapor-compression refrigeration devices optimized for high efficiency in both directions of thermal energy transfer. That is, heat pumps able to provide heating or cooling to the internal space as required.

task: wikipedia:Differential_(mechanical_device) (rev <2020-01-01)
text:
In automobiles and other wheeled vehicles, the differential allows the outer drive wheel to rotate faster than the inner drive wheel during a turn. This is necessary when the vehicle turns, making the wheel that is traveling around the outside of the turning curve roll farther and faster than the other. The average of the rotational speed of the two driving wheels equals the input rotational speed of the drive shaft. An increase in the speed of one wheel is balanced by a decrease in the speed of the other.

When used in this way, a differential couples the longitudinal input propeller shaft to the pinion, which in turn drives the transverse ring gear of the differential. This also usually works as reduction gearing. On rear wheel drive vehicles the differential may connect to half-shafts inside an axle housing, or drive shafts that connect to the rear driving wheels. Front wheel drive vehicles tend to have the engine crankshaft and the gearbox shafts transverse, and with the pinion on the end of the main-shaft of the gearbox and the differential enclosed in the same housing as the gearbox. There are individual drive-shafts to each wheel. A differential consists of one input, the drive shaft, and two outputs which are the two drive wheels, however the rotation of the drive wheels are coupled to each other by their connection to the roadway. Under normal conditions, with small tyre slip, the ratio of the speeds of the two driving wheels is defined by the ratio of the radii of the paths around which the two wheels are rolling, which in turn is determined by the track-width of the vehicle (the distance between the driving wheels) and the radius of the turn.

Non-automotive uses of differentials include performing analog arithmetic. Two of the differential's three shafts are made to rotate through angles that represent (are proportional to) two numbers, and the angle of the third shaft's rotation represents the sum or difference of the two input numbers. The earliest known use of a differential gear is in the Antikythera mechanism, circa 80 BCE, which used a differential gear to control a small sphere representing the moon from the difference between the sun and moon position pointers. The ball was painted black and white in hemispheres, and graphically showed the phase of the moon at a particular point in time. An equation clock that used a differential for addition was made in 1720. In the 20th Century, large assemblies of many differentials were used as analog computers, calculating, for example, the direction in which a gun should be aimed. However, the development of electronic digital computers has made these uses of differentials obsolete.

task: wikipedia:Cabin_pressurization (rev <2020-01-01)
text:
Cabin pressurization is a process in which conditioned air is pumped into the cabin of an aircraft or spacecraft, in order to create a safe and comfortable environment for passengers and crew flying at high altitudes. For aircraft, this air is usually bled off from the gas turbine engines at the compressor stage, and for spacecraft, it is carried in high-pressure, often cryogenic tanks. The air is cooled, humidified, and mixed with recirculated air if necessary, before it is distributed to the cabin by one or more environmental control systems. The cabin pressure is regulated by the outflow valve.

Pressurization becomes increasingly necessary at altitudes above  above sea level to protect crew and passengers from the risk of a number of physiological problems caused by the low outside air pressure above that altitude. For private aircraft operating in the US, crew members are required to use oxygen masks if the cabin altitude stays above 12,500 ft for more than 30 minutes, or if the cabin altitude reaches 14,000 ft at any time. At altitudes above 15,000 ft, passengers are required to be provided oxygen masks as well. On commercial aircraft, the cabin altitude must be maintained at  or less. Pressurization of the cargo hold is also required to prevent damage to pressure-sensitive goods that might leak, expand, burst or be crushed on re-pressurization. The principal physiological problems are listed below.

The pressure inside the cabin is technically referred to as the equivalent effective cabin altitude or more commonly as the cabin altitude. This is defined as the equivalent altitude above mean sea level having the same atmospheric pressure according to a standard atmospheric model such as the International Standard Atmosphere. Thus a cabin altitude of zero would have the pressure found at mean sea level, which is taken to be .

In airliners, cabin altitude during flight is kept above sea level in order to reduce stress on the pressurized part of the fuselage; this stress is proportional to the difference in pressure inside and outside the cabin. In a typical commercial passenger flight, the cabin altitude is programmed to rise gradually from the altitude of the airport of origin to a regulatory maximum of . This cabin altitude is maintained while the aircraft is cruising at its maximum altitude and then reduced gradually during descent until the cabin pressure matches the ambient air pressure at the destination.

task: wikipedia:Error_correction_code (rev <2020-01-01)
text:
In computing, telecommunication, information theory, and coding theory, an error correction code, sometimes error correcting code,  (ECC) is used for controlling errors in data over unreliable or noisy communication channels. The central idea is the sender encodes the message with a redundant in the form of an ECC. The American mathematician Richard Hamming pioneered this field in the 1940s and invented the first error-correcting code in 1950: the Hamming (7,4) code.
The redundancy allows the receiver to detect a limited number of errors that may occur anywhere in the message, and often to correct these errors without retransmission. ECC gives the receiver the ability to correct errors without needing a reverse channel to request retransmission of data, but at the cost of a fixed, higher forward channel bandwidth. ECC is therefore applied in situations where retransmissions are costly or impossible, such as one-way communication links and when transmitting to multiple receivers in multicast. For example, in the case of a satellite orbiting around Uranus, a retransmission because of decoding errors can create a delay of 5 hours. ECC information is usually added to mass storage devices to enable recovery of corrupted data, is widely used in modems, and is used on systems where the primary memory is ECC memory.

ECC processing in a receiver may be applied to a digital bit stream or in the demodulation of a digitally modulated carrier. For the latter, ECC is an integral part of the initial analog-to-digital conversion in the receiver. The Viterbi decoder implements a soft-decision algorithm to demodulate digital data from an analog signal corrupted by noise. Many ECC encoders/decoders can also generate a bit-error rate (BER) signal which can be used as feedback to fine-tune the analog receiving electronics.
 
The maximum fractions of errors or of missing bits that can be corrected is determined by the design of the ECC code, so different error correcting codes are suitable for different conditions. In general, a stronger code induces more redundancy that needs to be transmitted using the available bandwidth, which reduces the effective bit-rate while improving the received effective signal-to-noise ratio. The noisy-channel coding theorem of Claude Shannon answers the question of how much bandwidth is left for data communication while using the most efficient code that turns the decoding error probability to zero. This establishes bounds on the theoretical maximum information transfer rate of a channel with some given base noise level. However, the proof is not constructive, and hence gives no insight of how to build a capacity achieving code. After years of research, some advanced ECC systems nowadays  come very close to the theoretical maximum.

task: wikipedia:Laptop (rev <2020-01-01)
text:
A laptop (also laptop computer), often called a notebook, is a small, portable personal computer (PC) with a "clamshell" form factor, typically having a thin LCD or LED computer screen mounted on the inside of the upper lid of the clamshell and an alphanumeric keyboard on the inside of the lower lid. The clamshell is opened up to use the computer. Laptops are folded shut for transportation, and thus are suitable for mobile use. Its name comes from lap, as it was deemed to be placed on a person's lap when being used. Although originally there was a distinction between laptops and notebooks (the former being bigger and heavier than the latter), as of 2014, there is often no longer any difference. Laptops are commonly used in a variety of settings, such as at work, in education, for playing games, Internet surfing, for personal multimedia, and general home computer use.

Laptops combine all the input/output components and capabilities of a desktop computer, including the display screen, small speakers, a keyboard, hard disk drive, optical disc drive, pointing devices (such as a touchpad or trackpad), a processor, and memory into a single unit. Most modern laptops feature integrated webcams and built-in microphones, while many also have touchscreens. Laptops can be powered either from an internal battery or by an external power supply from an AC adapter. Hardware specifications, such as the processor speed and memory capacity, significantly vary between different types, makes, models and price points.

Design elements, form factor and construction can also vary significantly between models depending on intended use. Examples of specialized models of laptops include rugged notebooks for use in construction or military applications, as well as low production cost laptops such as those from the One Laptop per Child (OLPC) organization, which incorporate features like solar charging and semi-flexible components not found on most laptop computers. Portable computers, which later developed into modern laptops, were originally considered to be a small niche market, mostly for specialized field applications, such as in the military, for accountants, or for traveling sales representatives. As the portable computers evolved into the modern laptop, they became widely used for a variety of purposes.

The terms laptop and notebook are used interchangeably to describe a portable computer in English, although in some parts of the world one or the other may be preferred. There is some question as to the original etymology and specificity of either term—the term laptop appears to have been coined in the early 1980s to describe a mobile computer which could be used on one's lap, and to distinguish these devices from earlier, much heavier, portable computers (informally called "luggables").

Free public transport, often called fare-free public transit or zero-fare public transport, refers to public transport funded in full by means other than by collecting fares from passengers. It may be funded by national, regional or local government through taxation, or by commercial sponsorship by businesses.  Alternatively, the concept of "free-ness" may take other forms, such as no-fare access via a card which may or may not be paid for in its entirety by the user. Luxembourg is set to be the first country in the world to make all public transport free from 1 March 2020. Germany is considering making their public transit system fare-free in response to the EU's threatening to fine them for their air pollution levels.

Tallinn, capital city of Estonia with more than 420,000 inhabitants, and several mid-size European cities and many smaller towns around the world have converted their public transportation networks to zero-fare. The city of Hasselt in Belgium is a notable example: fares were abolished in 1997 and ridership was as much as "13 times higher" by 2006.

Local zero-fare shuttles or inner-city loops are far more common than citywide systems. They often use buses or trams. These may be set up by a city government to ease bottlenecks or fill short gaps in the transport network.

Some zero-fare services may be built to avoid the need for large transport construction. Port cities where shipping would require very high bridges might provide zero-fare ferries instead. These are free at the point of use, just as the use of a bridge might have been.
Machinery installed within a building or shopping centre can be seen as 'zero-fare transport': elevators, escalators and moving sidewalks are often provided by property owners and funded through the sales of goods and services. Community bicycle programs, providing free bicycles for short-term public use could be thought of as zero-fare transport.

A common example of zero-fare transport is student transport, where students travelling to or from school do not need to pay. A notable example is the University of Wisconsin-Stevens Point, which provides much of the funding to operate the Stevens Point Transit system. All students at the university can use any of the four citywide campus routes and the other four bus routes throughout the city free of charge. The university also funds two late night bus routes to serve the downtown free of charge with a goal of cutting down drunk driving.

task: wikipedia:Distance_education (rev <2020-01-01)
text:
Distance education or long-distance learning is the education of students who may not always be physically present at a school. Traditionally, this usually involved correspondence courses wherein the student corresponded with the school via post. Today it involves online education. A distance learning program can be completely distance learning, or a combination of distance learning and traditional classroom instruction (called hybrid or blended). Massive open online courses (MOOCs), offering large-scale interactive participation and open access through the World Wide Web or other network technologies, are recent developments in distance education. A number of other terms (distributed learning, e-learning, online learning, virtual classroom etc.) are used roughly synonymously with distance education.

One of the earliest attempts was advertised in 1728. This was in the Boston Gazette for "Caleb Philipps, Teacher of the new method of Short Hand", who sought students who wanted to learn through weekly mailed lessons.

The first distance education course in the modern sense was provided by Sir Isaac Pitman in the 1840s, who taught a system of shorthand by mailing texts transcribed into shorthand on postcards and receiving transcriptions from his students in return for correction. The element of student feedback was a crucial innovation of Pitman's system. This scheme was made possible by the introduction of uniform postage rates across England in 1840.

This early beginning proved extremely successful, and the Phonographic Correspondence Society was founded three years later to establish these courses on a more formal basis. The Society paved the way for the later formation of Sir Isaac Pitman Colleges across the country.

The University of London was the first university to offer distance learning degrees, establishing its External Programme in 1858. The background to this innovation lay in the fact that the institution (later known as University College London) was non-denominational and, given the intense religious rivalries at the time, there was an outcry against the "godless" university. The issue soon boiled down to which institutions had degree-granting powers and which institutions did not.

.|220x220px]]
The compromise solution that emerged in 1836 was that the sole authority to conduct the examinations leading to degrees would be given to a new officially recognized entity called the "University of London", which would act as examining body for the University of London colleges, originally University College London and King's College London, and award their students University of London degrees. As Sheldon Rothblatt states: "Thus arose in nearly archetypal form the famous English distinction between teaching and examining, here embodied in separate institutions."

task: Write instructions for replacing the chain on a bicycle.
text:
Shift the chain onto the smallest front chainring and the smallest rear sprocket. This releases most of the derailleur tension and makes removal easier. Clean the drivetrain first if it is heavily dirty, and gather a chain tool, a replacement chain compatible with your number of rear gears, master-link pliers if needed, and a rag. Wear gloves, since chain grease is difficult to remove.

If the old chain has a reusable quick link, rotate the pedals until the link is visible. Fit quick-link pliers into the link and squeeze to unlock it. If there is no quick link, use a chain tool to push out one rivet. Do not completely remove the rivet if you plan to reuse the chain, but for a replacement chain it is fine to separate it fully. Pull the chain away from the bicycle, noting how it passes through the rear derailleur’s two pulley wheels.

Compare the new chain with the old one by laying them side by side on a clean surface. Align one end of each chain and match the links at the opposite end. If the new chain is longer, remove the excess with the chain tool. If the old chain was badly stretched or the wrong length, determine the correct length by wrapping the new chain around the largest front chainring and largest rear sprocket, bypassing the derailleur. Add two complete links—one inner and one outer pair—then separate the chain at a suitable point. Never make the chain shorter than necessary.

Route the new chain through the rear derailleur carefully. It must pass over the upper pulley, between the derailleur cage plates, around the lower pulley, and then forward toward the chainring. Follow any guide tabs or diagrams printed on the derailleur; incorrect routing can cause rubbing or derailment.

Join the chain at the top of the chainstay using the supplied quick link or connecting rivet. For a quick link, insert both halves into the chain ends, then pull the chain firmly while applying pressure to seat the link. Some links require pliers or a firm pedal stroke to lock completely. For a connecting rivet, push it in with the chain tool until it is centered, then snap off the protruding guide section if applicable.

Turn the pedals by hand and shift through every gear. Check that the chain runs smoothly, the joining link is flexible, and the derailleur does not make unusual noise. Wipe off excess lubricant and apply a suitable bicycle chain lubricant to each roller.

task: Write instructions for replacing the chain on a bicycle.
text:
Wear safety glasses and gloves during this procedure. Keep your fingers away from the chainrings, sprockets, and derailleur.

Use a chain that matches the bicycle drivetrain. Check the number of speeds before you buy the chain. Use a chain tool for a chain with a connecting pin. Use quick-link pliers for a chain with a quick link.

1. Shift the chain onto the smallest front chainring and the smallest rear sprocket.
2. Set the bicycle on a repair stand.
3. Turn the pedals slowly and identify the chain connection.
4. Open the quick link with quick-link pliers, if the chain has a quick link.
5. Push the chain pin out with the chain tool, if the chain has a connecting pin.
6. Remove the chain from the bicycle.
7. Clean the chainrings, sprockets, and derailleur pulleys with a cloth.
8. Check the teeth for wear or damage.
9. Replace damaged parts before you install the new chain.

Compare the new chain with the old chain before you cut the new chain. Do not use a damaged or rusty chain.

1. Lay both chains on a clean surface.
2. Align one end of each chain.
3. Mark the new chain at the length of the old chain.
4. Make sure both chains have the same link count.
5. Cut the new chain at the marked link with the chain tool.
6. Remove the extra links from the new chain.
7. Route the new chain around the largest front chainring and the largest rear sprocket.
8. Keep the chain outside the rear derailleur.
9. Add two complete links to the chain length.
10. Cut the chain at that point if the old chain length was not correct.

A short chain can damage the derailleur. A long chain can shift poorly. Follow the chain maker’s length instructions when they differ from these steps.

1. Route the chain through the front derailleur cage.
2. Route the chain around the rear derailleur pulleys.
3. Check that the chain follows the guide plates on the derailleur.
4. Connect the chain with a new quick link or a new connecting pin.
5. Follow the connection part instructions.
6. Turn the pedals backward to place the connection at the top.
7. Pull the rear brake and press the pedals firmly to lock a quick link.
8. Check the connecting pin position on both outer plates.
9. Remove any chain stiffness at the connection by flexing the chain sideways.
10. Turn the pedals forward through several complete turns.
11. Shift through all rear sprockets and front chainrings.
12. Make sure the chain moves smoothly and does not fall off.
13. Wipe excess lubricant from the chain.
14. Apply bicycle chain lubricant to each chain roller.

task: Write instructions for replacing the chain on a bicycle.
text:
Shift the chain onto the smallest chainring and the smallest rear cog. This takes tension off the derailleur and makes the job less awkward. If the chain is filthy, wipe it down first. You don’t need it spotless, but you should be able to see the connecting link.

Find the chain’s joining point. Many chains use a reusable quick link, which looks slightly different from the other links. Others are joined with a special pin. If there’s a quick link, squeeze it with quick-link pliers, or press the pedals while holding the rear brake to help release it. Don’t force it sideways with a screwdriver unless you’re stuck; that can damage the plates.

For a chain joined by a pin, use a chain tool. Push the pin out carefully, but don’t remove it completely if you’re working with a reusable rivet-style chain. Most replacement chains come with their own joining pin or quick link, so check the instructions that came with it.

Lay the old chain beside the new one on a clean surface. Match them link for link, then mark where the new chain needs to end. If the old chain was badly stretched or the gearing has changed, use the big-chainring-to-big-cog method instead: route the new chain around both largest sprockets, bypassing the rear derailleur, then add two complete links. That usually gives the correct length.

Use the chain tool to remove the extra links. Make sure you’re removing them from the correct end, since some chains have a specific directional orientation. If the chain is marked with arrows or a logo, follow those markings.

Route the new chain through the rear derailleur. It should pass over the upper jockey wheel, then between the derailleur cage plates and around the lower wheel. This is the part people get wrong, usually because they rush it. Reconnect the chain while it’s still looped through the derailleur, using the supplied quick link or joining pin.

Turn the cranks slowly by hand. Watch that the chain settles onto every tooth and that the derailleur cage moves normally. Shift through the gears one at a time, then wipe off excess lubricant. A fresh chain shouldn’t be dripping wet with oil. Finally, take a short, gentle ride and listen for clicking or skipping. If it skips under pressure, stop riding and check the connection and chain length before it causes trouble.

task: Write instructions for jump-starting a car with jumper cables.
text:
Before starting, move both vehicles to a safe, well-ventilated location away from traffic. Turn off both engines, set the parking brakes, place automatic transmissions in Park or manual transmissions in neutral, and switch off lights, radios, heaters, and other accessories. Do not attempt to jump-start a vehicle with a cracked, leaking, swollen, or frozen battery. Keep cigarettes, flames, and metal jewelry away from the batteries. Check the owner’s manuals first, especially for hybrid, electric, or newer vehicles, because some require designated jump points or special procedures. Confirm that both vehicles use compatible 12-volt systems.

Park the vehicles close enough for the cables to reach, but do not let them touch. Open the hoods and locate the positive (+) and negative (–) terminals or the manufacturer-marked jump points. Untangle the jumper cables, keeping the clamps separated so they cannot touch each other.

1. Attach the red clamp to the positive (+) terminal of the dead battery.
2. Attach the other red clamp to the positive (+) terminal of the working battery.
3. Attach the black clamp to the negative (–) terminal of the working battery.
4. Attach the remaining black clamp to an unpainted, solid metal part of the disabled vehicle’s engine block or chassis, away from the battery, fuel lines, and moving components. This reduces the chance of a spark near battery gases.

Confirm that all four clamps are firmly attached and that the cables are clear of belts, fans, and pulleys. Start the vehicle with the working battery and let it run for several minutes. Then try starting the disabled vehicle. Do not crank for more than about 10 seconds at a time; if it does not start, wait a minute before trying again and check the connections. Stop if you see sparks, smell fuel, or notice smoke.

Once the disabled vehicle starts, let both engines run for a few minutes. Disconnect the cables in reverse order: black clamp from the disabled vehicle’s metal ground, black clamp from the donor battery, red clamp from the donor battery, and finally red clamp from the revived vehicle. Do not allow the clamps to touch. Keep the revived vehicle running or drive it for at least 20–30 minutes, then have the battery and charging system tested if it fails to restart.

task: Write instructions for jump-starting a car with jumper cables.
text:
Jumper Cable Procedure

Read the vehicle manual before you use jumper cables.  
Use this procedure only when both vehicles have the same battery voltage.  
Do not use jumper cables if either battery has a crack, a leak, or frozen electrolyte.  
Park the vehicles close enough for the cables to reach, but do not let them touch.  
Set both parking brakes and move both transmissions to PARK or NEUTRAL.  
Turn off both engines and all electrical equipment.

WARNING: A battery can release flammable gas.  
Keep cigarettes, flames, and sparks away from both batteries.  
Wear safety glasses and protective gloves when you handle the cables.  
Do not connect a damaged cable or allow the cable clamps to touch.

1. Open both engine compartments.
2. Find the positive and negative battery terminals on both vehicles.
3. Remove dirt from the terminals with a dry cloth.
4. Find the vehicle manufacturer’s designated connection points if the battery terminals are not accessible.
5. Put the red cable near the positive terminals.
6. Put the black cable near the negative terminal on the support vehicle.
7. Connect one red clamp to the positive terminal of the discharged battery.
8. Connect the other red clamp to the positive terminal of the support battery.
9. Connect one black clamp to the negative terminal of the support battery.
10. Connect the other black clamp to clean, unpainted metal on the disabled vehicle.
11. Select a metal point away from the battery, the fuel system, and moving parts.
12. Do not connect the last black clamp to the discharged battery’s negative terminal.
13. Keep the cable clamps away from fans, belts, pulleys, and other moving parts.

Start the engine of the support vehicle.  
Let the engine operate for one minute.  
Start the engine of the disabled vehicle.  
Stop and check the cable connections if the engine does not start.  
Wait several minutes before you try again.  
Do not make more than three start attempts.

Disconnect the cables in the reverse order of connection.  
Remove the black clamp from the disabled vehicle’s metal point.  
Remove the black clamp from the support battery.  
Remove the red clamp from the support battery.  
Remove the red clamp from the disabled vehicle.  
Do not let any clamp touch a terminal or metal part during removal.

Keep the engine of the recovered vehicle on for at least 20 minutes.  
Drive the vehicle to charge the battery if the vehicle operates normally.  
Stop the vehicle and get technical assistance if the engine stops again.  
Have the battery and the charging system tested as soon as possible.

task: Write instructions for jump-starting a car with jumper cables.
text:
Park the working car close enough to reach the dead car with the cables, but don’t let the vehicles touch. Turn both engines off, put both cars in Park or Neutral, set the parking brakes, and switch off lights, radios, and other electrical accessories.

Before connecting anything, check the batteries. Don’t try to jump a battery that’s cracked, leaking, badly swollen, or frozen. That can be dangerous. Also check the owner’s manual, especially if either vehicle is a hybrid, electric car, or has a special jump-start terminal. Some cars shouldn’t be connected directly to the battery.

Untangle the jumper cables and keep the metal clamps from touching each other. Identify the red cable as positive and the black cable as negative. Connect them in this order:

1. Attach one red clamp to the positive (+) terminal of the dead battery.
2. Attach the other red clamp to the positive (+) terminal of the working battery.
3. Attach one black clamp to the negative (−) terminal of the working battery.
4. Attach the last black clamp to an unpainted metal part of the dead car’s engine block or chassis, away from the battery and moving parts.

That final connection may spark a little, which is why it should be made away from the battery. Don’t clip the black clamp onto the dead battery’s negative terminal unless the vehicle’s instructions specifically tell you to.

Start the working car and let it run for a minute or two. Then try starting the dead car. Don’t crank it continuously. If it doesn’t start after about five seconds, stop and wait a minute before trying again. A few attempts are reasonable; repeated cranking usually means the battery isn’t the only problem.

Once the dead car starts, leave both engines running for several minutes. Then remove the cables in reverse order: black clamp from the previously dead car, black clamp from the working car, red clamp from the working car, and finally red clamp from the revived car. Keep the clamps from touching any metal or each other while they’re connected.

Drive the revived car for at least 20 to 30 minutes, preferably somewhere you won’t get stranded. If it dies again, starts slowly, or the battery warning light stays on, have the battery and charging system tested. The battery may simply be worn out, or the alternator may not be charging it.

task: Write instructions for bleeding air from a hydraulic disc brake.
text:
Before beginning, identify the brake-fluid type specified by the manufacturer: DOT fluid and mineral oil are not interchangeable. Use the correct bleed kit, fresh fluid from a sealed container, gloves, eye protection, shop towels, and the tools required for the caliper and lever bleed ports. Work in a clean, well-ventilated area, and keep fluid away from brake pads, rotors, paint, and rubber parts.

1. Remove the wheel if necessary, then remove the brake pads. Insert the manufacturer’s pad spacer or a suitable bleed block so the pistons cannot move outward. If fluid has contaminated the pads, replace them rather than trying to clean them.

2. Position the brake lever so its reservoir or bleed port is level and accessible. Secure the bicycle or vehicle firmly. Remove the bleed-port screw carefully, avoiding dirt entering the reservoir. Install the appropriate syringe, funnel, hose, or collection bottle according to the brake design.

3. At the caliper, remove the rubber cap from the bleed nipple and fit the bleed hose. Place the other end in a container. Fill the syringe with the specified fresh fluid, eliminating air bubbles before connecting it. Do not allow the syringe to run empty while pushing fluid through the system.

4. Open the caliper bleed nipple slightly, usually about one-quarter turn, and slowly push fluid from the caliper toward the lever if the manufacturer specifies a reverse bleed. Otherwise, use the prescribed direction. Watch for bubbles emerging into the funnel, syringe, or collection bottle. Lightly tap the hose, caliper, and lever body to release trapped air.

5. Continue until clear, bubble-free fluid flows through the system. Gently squeeze and release the lever several times, pausing between strokes, while keeping the reservoir supplied. Do not pull the lever to the handlebar if the manufacturer warns against it.

6. Close the bleed nipple while fluid is still moving, then remove the hose and refit the cap. Top up the reservoir if needed and reinstall the bleed-port screw with its seal. Clean every trace of spilled fluid using the recommended cleaner; never spray cleaner directly onto seals.

7. Refit the clean, unworn pads and wheel. Pump the lever until it feels firm, check carefully for leaks, and verify that the rotor is centered without rubbing. Dispose of used fluid responsibly, never pour it down a drain. If the lever remains spongy or fluid leaks, do not ride; repeat the procedure or have a qualified technician inspect the brake.

task: Write instructions for bleeding air from a hydraulic disc brake.
text:
Wear protective gloves and eye protection before you service the hydraulic disc brake.

Use only the brake fluid that the brake manufacturer specifies.  
Do not mix DOT fluid with mineral oil.  
Keep brake fluid away from the brake pads, rotor, paint, and plastic parts.  
Replace contaminated brake pads.  
Use a clean container, a clear drain tube, a bleed wrench, and fresh brake fluid.

1. Put the bicycle on a stable stand.  
2. Turn the handlebar until the brake fluid reservoir sits level.  
3. Remove dirt from the reservoir cover and the caliper bleed screw.  
4. Remove the wheel if the manufacturer gives this instruction.  
5. Remove the brake pads if fluid can reach them.  
6. Install a pad spacer in the caliper.

Warning: Do not pull the brake lever after you remove the wheel or the brake pads.

7. Remove the reservoir cover and the diaphragm.  
8. Fill the reservoir with the specified brake fluid.  
9. Push the clear drain tube onto the caliper bleed screw.  
10. Put the other end of the tube into the clean container.  
11. Keep the tube end below the fluid level in the container.  
12. Loosen the bleed screw one quarter turn.

13. Pull the brake lever slowly two or three times.  
14. Hold the lever against the handlebar.  
15. Close the bleed screw before you release the lever.  
16. Release the lever slowly.  
17. Check the fluid level in the reservoir.  
18. Add fluid before the reservoir becomes empty.

Caution: Do not let air enter the reservoir or the brake system.

19. Repeat the lever cycle until the tube shows no air bubbles.  
20. Tap the brake hose and caliper gently with a plastic handle.  
21. Repeat the lever cycle to move trapped air toward the reservoir.  
22. Keep the reservoir full during the complete procedure.  
23. Close the bleed screw when clean fluid leaves the tube.  
24. Remove the tube from the bleed screw.  
25. Tighten the bleed screw to the specified torque.

26. Fill the reservoir to the specified level.  
27. Install the diaphragm and the reservoir cover.  
28. Clean spilled fluid from the caliper and brake hose.  
29. Install clean brake pads and the wheel.  
30. Pump the brake lever until the pads contact the rotor.  
31. Check that the lever feels firm and does not contact the handlebar.  
32. Check the bleed screw, hose, and reservoir for fluid leaks.  
33. Test the brake at low speed in a safe area.  
34. Do not ride the bicycle if the brake feels soft or shows a leak.

task: Write instructions for bleeding air from a hydraulic disc brake.
text:
Put the bike or vehicle on a stand so the master cylinder reservoir sits level. Read the brake manufacturer’s instructions first, because some systems use DOT fluid and others use mineral oil. They aren’t interchangeable. Use only the specified fluid, and wear gloves and eye protection. Brake fluid damages paint, plastic, and some finishes.

Remove the wheel if it’s a bicycle, then take out the brake pads. Keep the pads far away from fluid. If any oil or brake fluid touches them, replace them rather than trying to save them. Insert a bleed block or another suitable spacer between the pistons so they can’t move while you work.

Clean the reservoir and caliper thoroughly. Dirt getting inside the system can cause trouble later. Remove the reservoir cover or bleed screw, depending on the brake design, and place an absorbent cloth underneath. At the caliper, push a snug piece of clear bleed hose onto the bleed nipple. Put the other end into a container. A syringe may be required for some bicycle brakes, while automotive systems commonly use a hose and catch bottle.

Open the bleed nipple slightly, usually about a quarter turn. Don’t remove it. Slowly squeeze and release the brake lever or pedal. Watch the hose and reservoir. Air bubbles should travel out with the old fluid. Keep the reservoir from running dry, because that pulls more air into the system and means you’ll have to start again. Add fresh fluid as needed.

Continue until the fluid coming through is clean and bubble-free. Tap the hose, caliper, and master cylinder lightly with a plastic handle to loosen bubbles stuck to the walls. On a car, have an assistant press the pedal while you close the nipple, then release the pedal. Never let the pedal come back up while the nipple is open. Repeat the press, hold, open, close sequence until no bubbles appear.

Close the bleed nipple firmly, but don’t overtighten it. Remove the hose and clean every trace of fluid from the caliper. Fill the reservoir to its marked level and refit the cover, or install the specified bleed screw and seal.

Pump the lever or pedal several times. It should feel firm, not spongy or increasingly soft. Check carefully for leaks, reinstall the pads and wheel, and make sure the rotor is clean. Test the brake at walking speed in a safe area before riding or driving normally. If the lever still feels soft, stop and bleed it again or have a qualified mechanic inspect it.

task: Write instructions for replacing a kitchen faucet cartridge.
text:
Turn off the water supply before beginning. Look beneath the sink for two shutoff valves, one for hot water and one for cold water, and turn both clockwise until they stop. Open the faucet to release pressure and confirm that no water flows. Place a towel or shallow container in the cabinet to catch drips, and close the drain or cover it so small parts cannot fall inside.

Remove the faucet handle. Depending on the design, the handle may have a decorative cap covering the screw, a small set screw on the side, or a retaining screw beneath the handle. Pry off a cap gently with a thin flat screwdriver, if necessary, then loosen the screw with the correct screwdriver or hex key. Pull the handle straight upward. If it is stuck, rock it gently from side to side; avoid forcing it, because the faucet body or valve stem can be damaged.

With the handle removed, identify the retaining nut, clip, or collar holding the cartridge in place. Unscrew the nut counterclockwise with adjustable pliers or a wrench, protecting the finish with a cloth. If a metal retaining clip is present, pull it out carefully with needle-nose pliers. Keep track of the order and orientation of all parts as you remove them.

Grip the cartridge stem with pliers and pull the cartridge straight out. If it will not move, use a cartridge-pulling tool designed for your faucet brand. Do not twist aggressively or pry against the faucet body. Remove and discard the old cartridge, then clean mineral deposits and debris from the valve opening with a cloth.

Compare the replacement cartridge with the old one to ensure the size, stem shape, and locating tabs match. Coat the cartridge’s rubber seals lightly with plumber’s silicone grease, not petroleum jelly. Insert it in the same orientation as the original, aligning its tabs with the slots in the valve body. Reinstall the retaining clip, nut, collar, and handle in reverse order. Tighten firmly but do not overtighten.

Reopen both shutoff valves slowly. Turn on the faucet and let cold and hot water run for several minutes to flush debris. Check around the cartridge and supply connections for leaks. If water drips from the handle or the faucet operates backward, shut off the valves and verify the cartridge orientation, seals, and retaining hardware.

task: Write instructions for replacing a kitchen faucet cartridge.
text:
A faucet cartridge controls the water flow and temperature inside the faucet body. Replace the cartridge when the faucet drips after you close the handle. Use a cartridge that matches the faucet model and the old cartridge. Read the faucet manufacturer's instructions before you remove any parts.

Warning: Water pressure can move parts and cause water to spray from the faucet. Make sure that you can reach both shutoff valves under the sink. Put a container below the faucet to collect water. Wear safety glasses when you work below the sink.

Prepare these tools and materials:

- A replacement cartridge
- An adjustable wrench
- A hex key set
- A screwdriver set
- Slip-joint pliers
- A clean cloth
- Silicone plumber's grease
- A small container

1. Turn the handle to the center position.
2. Turn the hot and cold shutoff valves clockwise.
3. Open the faucet handle to release water pressure.
4. Close the faucet handle after the water stops.
5. Put the container below the faucet body.
6. Cover the drain with the cloth or a drain stopper.
7. Remove the handle cap with a thin screwdriver.
8. Remove the handle screw with the correct screwdriver or hex key.
9. Pull the handle straight up from the faucet stem.
10. Wrap the cloth around the retaining nut.
11. Turn the retaining nut counterclockwise with the adjustable wrench.
12. Remove the retaining nut from the faucet body.
13. Remove the cartridge clip with the screwdriver or pliers, if the faucet has a clip.
14. Pull the old cartridge straight up with the pliers.
15. Turn the cartridge gently if it does not move.
16. Do not use strong force because you can damage the faucet body.
17. Clean the cartridge opening with the cloth.
18. Remove mineral deposits from the opening with a soft brush.
19. Compare the new cartridge with the old cartridge.
20. Align the tabs on the new cartridge with the slots in the faucet body.
21. Push the new cartridge fully into the faucet body.
22. Install the cartridge clip, if the faucet has a clip.
23. Apply a thin layer of silicone plumber's grease to the retaining nut threads.
24. Install the retaining nut by hand.
25. Tighten the retaining nut with the wrench.
26. Do not overtighten the nut because excessive force can damage the cartridge.
27. Install the handle on the faucet stem.
28. Install and tighten the handle screw.
29. Press the handle cap into its opening.
30. Turn the shutoff valves counterclockwise.
31. Open the faucet slowly.
32. Check the faucet and the shutoff valves for leaks.
33. Close the faucet and wait for one minute.
34. Check the faucet again for water leaks.
35. Remove the container and the cloth after you find no leaks.

task: Write instructions for replacing a kitchen faucet cartridge.
text:
Turn off the water supply before touching the faucet. Look under the sink for the two small shutoff valves and turn them clockwise until they stop. Open the faucet to release pressure, then cover the drain with a stopper or rag so a tiny screw doesn’t disappear down the pipes.

Put a towel in the cabinet, too. Some water will still come out when you remove the cartridge, and it always seems to find the one dry spot you forgot to protect.

Remove the faucet handle. The screw may be hidden under a decorative cap, behind a small plug, or beneath a set screw on the side of the handle. Pry off a cap gently with a thin flat screwdriver, or loosen the set screw with the correct Allen key. Don’t force it. If the handle won’t lift after the screw is out, wiggle it from side to side. A handle puller may be necessary if mineral buildup has practically welded it in place.

With the handle removed, take off the retaining nut, clip, or bonnet holding the cartridge in the faucet body. Use an adjustable wrench, but wrap the nut with a cloth first to protect the finish. Some faucets have a U-shaped retaining clip that slides out with pliers. Keep track of which way it’s positioned.

Pull the old cartridge straight up. If it refuses to move, rock it gently or use a cartridge-pulling tool made for that faucet brand. Avoid prying hard against the faucet body; cracked plumbing is a much bigger job than a stuck cartridge.

Before installing the replacement, wipe the inside of the faucet body clean. Compare the new cartridge with the old one, especially the stem shape and alignment tabs. Rub a thin layer of silicone plumber’s grease on the cartridge’s O-rings. Don’t use petroleum jelly, which can damage some rubber seals.

Slide the new cartridge into place, matching the tabs and grooves. Reinstall the retaining clip or nut and tighten it firmly, but don’t crank on it. Put the handle back on and secure its screw or cap.

Turn the shutoff valves on slowly. Check underneath for leaks, then run the faucet from cold to hot for a minute to flush out grit. If water still drips from the spout, the cartridge may be misaligned, the wrong model, or not seated completely. Shut the water off again before taking it apart.

task: Explain how a heat pump moves heat against a temperature gradient.
text:
A heat pump moves heat from a colder region to a warmer one by using external energy, usually electricity, to drive a refrigeration cycle. This does not violate the second law of thermodynamics because the system is not moving heat “for free”; work is supplied to force heat in the thermodynamically unfavorable direction.

The cycle begins in the evaporator, located on the cold side. A refrigerant at low pressure flows through this heat exchanger. Because its boiling point is very low at that pressure, it evaporates even when the surrounding air, ground, or water is relatively cold. During evaporation, the refrigerant absorbs thermal energy from its surroundings. The absorbed heat raises the refrigerant’s energy and changes it from a liquid into a vapor, but its temperature can remain below the temperature of the heat source.

The vapor then enters a compressor. The compressor does mechanical work on it, squeezing the vapor into a smaller volume. Compression increases both the refrigerant’s pressure and its temperature. This is the crucial step that allows the refrigerant to release heat to a warmer environment: after compression, its temperature is higher than that of the building’s indoor air or another heat sink.

The hot, high-pressure vapor passes through the condenser. There, it transfers energy to the warm side, such as a house’s radiators, underfloor pipes, or air distribution system. As the refrigerant loses heat, it condenses back into a high-pressure liquid. The heat delivered by the condenser includes not only the work added by the compressor but also the heat originally collected from the cold source.

Finally, the liquid travels through an expansion valve. The valve sharply reduces its pressure, causing its temperature to fall and preparing it to absorb heat again in the evaporator. The cycle then repeats continuously.

Thus, a heat pump does not create heat or simply “pull” it uphill. It uses a compressor and a circulating refrigerant to manipulate pressure and phase changes, making it possible to absorb heat at a low temperature and reject it at a higher temperature. Its efficiency is described by the coefficient of performance: the heat delivered divided by the electrical work consumed. Because the system moves existing heat rather than generating all of it directly, a heat pump can deliver several units of heat for each unit of electricity under favorable conditions.

task: Explain how a heat pump moves heat against a temperature gradient.
text:
Heat normally moves from a warmer area to a colder area. This movement follows the temperature gradient. A heat pump moves heat in the opposite direction. It moves heat from a cold source to a warmer space. The pump needs energy to perform this task.

The heat pump uses a refrigerant as a heat transfer fluid. The refrigerant changes between a liquid and a vapor. These changes allow the refrigerant to absorb and release large amounts of heat. A closed circuit carries the refrigerant through the heat pump. The circuit has four main parts.

1. The evaporator receives heat from the cold source. The source can be outdoor air, ground, or water. The refrigerant has a lower temperature than the source. Heat moves from the source into the refrigerant. The refrigerant changes from a liquid to a vapor.

2. The compressor receives the vapor from the evaporator. The compressor applies mechanical energy to the vapor. This action increases the vapor pressure and temperature. The hot, high-pressure vapor then moves to the condenser. The compressor supplies the main energy input for the heat pump.

3. The condenser transfers heat to the warm space. The refrigerant temperature is higher than the space temperature. Heat moves from the refrigerant into the space. The refrigerant changes from a vapor to a liquid. The released heat can warm a room or heat water.

4. The expansion valve receives the high-pressure liquid. The valve reduces the liquid pressure. The refrigerant temperature decreases as the pressure decreases. The cold refrigerant then moves back to the evaporator. The cycle starts again.

The compressor creates the pressure difference that permits this cycle. The low pressure in the evaporator keeps the refrigerant cold. The high pressure in the condenser makes the refrigerant hot. This pressure difference controls the direction of heat transfer. The refrigerant does not move heat because it moves by itself.

A heat pump can also provide cooling. A reversing valve changes the refrigerant flow direction. The indoor coil then removes heat from the room. The outdoor coil releases that heat to the air or ground. The same basic parts perform the opposite function.

The heat pump does not produce all its output heat from electrical energy. It moves most of the heat from the source. Electrical energy operates the compressor and other components. Therefore, the heat output can be greater than the electrical input. The system still obeys the temperature gradient because external energy drives the heat transfer.

task: Explain how a heat pump moves heat against a temperature gradient.
text:
A heat pump moves heat from a colder place to a warmer one by using energy, usually electricity, to run a refrigeration cycle. That sounds like it breaks the rules of thermodynamics. It doesn’t. Heat naturally flows downhill, from high temperature to low temperature, but a heat pump supplies work so heat can be pushed uphill.

The process begins in the outdoor coil, called the evaporator. A special fluid, the refrigerant, flows through it at low pressure. Because its boiling point falls when pressure falls, the refrigerant can evaporate even when the outdoor air is chilly. As it changes from liquid to vapor, it absorbs heat from the surrounding air or ground. In winter, this is where the heat pump collects energy, even if the air feels cold to you.

The vapor then enters the compressor. This is the part that uses electrical power. The compressor squeezes the refrigerant into a much smaller volume, raising both its pressure and its temperature. The resulting hot, high-pressure vapor travels to the indoor coil, or condenser.

Inside the building, the refrigerant is hotter than the room air. Heat therefore flows from the refrigerant into the house, warming the air or heating water in a radiant system. As it loses heat, the refrigerant condenses back into a liquid. The heat hasn’t appeared from nowhere; some came from outdoors, and some of the input electricity ended up as heat as well.

Next, the liquid passes through an expansion valve. The valve restricts its flow, causing a sharp drop in pressure and temperature. The refrigerant is now cold enough to absorb heat again, so it returns to the outdoor evaporator and the cycle repeats.

The clever part is the pressure change. By compressing the refrigerant, the pump makes it hot enough to release heat indoors. By expanding it afterward, the system makes it cold enough to collect heat outdoors. A valve can reverse the refrigerant’s direction, allowing the same machine to cool a building in summer.

A heat pump doesn’t create heat in the way a furnace burns fuel. It relocates heat, and the electricity pays for the uphill move. That’s why it can deliver several units of heat for each unit of electrical energy, especially when the temperature difference between indoors and outdoors isn’t extreme.

task: Explain how a differential lets a car's wheels turn at different speeds.
text:
When a car turns, its inside and outside wheels follow different paths. The outside wheel travels along a larger circle, so it must cover more distance than the inside wheel. If both wheels were permanently locked to the same axle and forced to rotate at the same speed, one would have to slip across the road. This would cause tire scrubbing, steering difficulty, noise, and increased wear.

A differential solves this problem by allowing the two driven wheels to rotate at different speeds while still receiving power from the engine. Power travels through the transmission and driveshaft to the final drive, where a small pinion gear turns a larger ring gear. The ring gear is attached to the differential carrier, a housing that contains several smaller bevel gears.

Inside the carrier are usually two “side gears,” connected to the left and right axle shafts, and two or more “spider gears,” mounted on a cross-shaped support. When the car travels straight, both wheels encounter similar resistance and rotate at the same speed. In this situation, the carrier turns the spider gears around the side gears, but the spider gears do not need to spin significantly on their own axles. Both side gears therefore turn together.

During a turn, resistance differs between the wheels. The outside wheel needs to rotate faster, while the inside wheel needs to rotate more slowly. The spider gears begin spinning on their own mounting shafts as they orbit with the carrier. Their motion allows one side gear to speed up by exactly as much as the other side gear slows down. The carrier continues supplying torque to both axle shafts, but the wheels are no longer forced to match speeds.

For example, if the carrier turns at a certain average speed, the differential may let the outside wheel rotate ten revolutions per minute faster and the inside wheel ten revolutions per minute slower. Their average speed remains tied to the carrier’s speed.

A standard open differential works well on normal roads, but it can send most available torque to a wheel that has little grip. Limited-slip and locking differentials reduce or prevent this behavior for better traction off-road, in performance driving, or on slippery surfaces.

task: Explain how a differential lets a car's wheels turn at different speeds.
text:
A differential is a gear unit in the drive axle. It sends engine torque to two drive wheels. It also lets each wheel turn at a different speed. This function is important when the car turns.

The outer wheel travels a longer path than the inner wheel during a turn. Both wheels touch the road, so each wheel must cover its own path. The outer wheel must turn faster than the inner wheel. The difference in wheel speed increases when the turn becomes tighter.

The differential uses a carrier, side gears, and pinion gears. The drive shaft turns the ring gear through the final drive. The ring gear turns the carrier. The carrier holds the pinion gears and makes them move around the side gears. Each side gear connects to one axle shaft and one drive wheel.

When the car moves straight, the pinion gears do not rotate around their own shafts. The carrier turns both side gears at the same speed. Both wheels then turn at the same speed. The differential still sends torque through both axle shafts.

When the car turns, the pinion gears rotate on their own shafts. This rotation lets one side gear turn faster and the other side gear turn slower. The outer wheel then turns faster than the inner wheel. The carrier continues to send torque to both side gears. The gears change wheel speed without forcing both wheels to follow the same path.

An open differential gives a useful result on a dry road. It helps prevent tire scrub and reduces stress in the axle shafts. Tire scrub occurs when a tire slides because its speed does not match its path. The differential reduces this slide during a turn. It also helps the car turn smoothly.

An open differential has a limit when one wheel loses grip. The wheel with less grip can spin quickly. The other wheel can then receive only the torque that the slipping wheel can use. The car may not move, even when the other wheel has good grip. A limited-slip differential reduces this problem with extra clutch plates or special gears. A locking differential can connect both axle shafts and force similar wheel speeds. These systems help the car move on loose ground, but they can increase tire wear during tight turns.

task: Explain how a differential lets a car's wheels turn at different speeds.
text:
When a car turns, the outside wheel travels farther than the inside wheel. Picture two wheels on the same axle going around a bend: the outer one traces a bigger circle, while the inner one follows a smaller circle. If both wheels were locked together and forced to rotate at exactly the same speed, one of them would have to slip across the pavement.

That’s what the differential prevents.

Power leaves the transmission through the driveshaft and reaches a small gear called the pinion. The pinion turns a much larger ring gear, which is attached to the differential housing. Inside that housing are several smaller gears, usually called spider gears, that mesh with gears connected to the two axle shafts. Those axle shafts drive the left and right wheels.

When the car is moving straight, the differential’s internal gears don’t need to rotate around their own little axes. The whole assembly turns together, sending equal speed to both wheels. The wheels cover the same distance, so that arrangement works fine.

During a turn, things change. The spider gears start rotating inside the housing, allowing one side gear, and therefore one wheel, to speed up while the other slows down. The outside wheel might rotate at 1,000 revolutions per minute and the inside wheel at 800, depending on the turn. The differential itself handles that difference smoothly, without forcing either tire to drag.

You can think of it as sharing rotation rather than dividing it rigidly. In a basic, open differential, the average speed of the two axle shafts matches the speed of the differential housing. If one wheel speeds up by 100 rpm, the other slows down by roughly 100 rpm.

There’s a catch. An open differential sends torque through the path of least resistance. If one tire is on ice or lifted off the ground, it can spin while the tire with grip receives very little useful power. That’s why some cars use limited-slip differentials, locking differentials, or electronic systems that brake a spinning wheel.

Without a differential, turning would be jerky, tires would scrub against the road, and the axle would suffer unnecessary stress. With one, the wheels can follow their separate paths while the engine keeps driving both.

task: Explain why aircraft cabins are pressurized and how the system works.
text:
Aircraft cabins are pressurized because atmospheric pressure falls sharply as altitude increases. At a typical cruising altitude of 35,000 feet, the outside air contains roughly the same percentage of oxygen as at sea level, about 21 percent, but the air is much less dense. Consequently, each breath supplies too few oxygen molecules to support normal human performance. Without protection, passengers and crew would quickly experience hypoxia, causing impaired judgment, unconsciousness, and potentially death. Low pressure would also make body fluids and gases expand and would create uncomfortable or dangerous conditions.

Cabin pressurization does not usually recreate sea-level pressure completely. Most airliners maintain a cabin altitude of approximately 6,000 to 8,000 feet, even while the aircraft is flying far higher. This setting reduces stress on the fuselage and saves fuel compared with maintaining sea-level pressure, while still providing enough oxygen for healthy occupants. Some newer aircraft, particularly those with composite structures, can maintain a lower cabin altitude and higher humidity for improved comfort.

The system begins with outside air entering the engines. In many jet aircraft, compressors extract some pressurized air from intermediate or high compressor stages before combustion; this is called bleed air. Other designs use electrically driven compressors. The hot, compressed air passes through an air-conditioning pack, where it is cooled, dried or managed for humidity, and expanded to a suitable pressure and temperature. A portion of the conditioned air is mixed with recirculated cabin air that has passed through filters. This mixture is continuously delivered through ducts, while fresh air replaces cabin air several times per hour.

A pressure controller regulates the cabin by controlling an outflow valve, usually located near the rear of the aircraft. Inflow is generally supplied at a controlled rate, and the valve adjusts how much air leaves. Closing it raises cabin pressure; opening it lowers pressure. During climb, the controller changes pressure gradually to prevent ear discomfort. During descent, it increases outside pressure inside the cabin in a similarly controlled way so that the cabin reaches near-ambient pressure before landing.

Multiple independent safety features protect against malfunction. Positive-pressure relief valves prevent excessive pressure that could damage the fuselage, while negative-pressure valves admit outside air if cabin pressure would otherwise become higher than the external pressure. Warning systems alert the crew to low pressure, and emergency oxygen masks deploy if cabin altitude becomes dangerously high. In a rapid decompression, the masks provide oxygen while the pilots descend promptly to a safer altitude. Thus, pressurization balances human physiology, aircraft strength, comfort, and operational safety.

task: Explain why aircraft cabins are pressurized and how the system works.
text:
Aircraft fly at high altitude to reduce air resistance and fuel use. At high altitude, the outside air has low pressure and low oxygen density. Human lungs cannot receive enough oxygen from this air without assistance. The pressurization system keeps the cabin pressure at a safe level for passengers and crew. It also prevents discomfort and injury from large pressure changes.

The system does not usually keep the cabin at sea-level pressure. A high pressure difference would put extra loads on the fuselage, windows, doors, and seals. The system uses a cabin altitude that gives enough oxygen for normal activity. The aircraft flight manual gives the maximum cabin altitude and pressure difference.

The engines supply hot, compressed air to the air conditioning packs. Some aircraft use electric compressors instead of engine air. The packs cool the air and control its temperature. The packs send the conditioned air into the cabin through ducts. A recirculation system filters some cabin air and mixes it with fresh air.

The cabin pressure controller controls the pressure inside the cabin. The controller receives data from pressure sensors, the aircraft altitude, and the selected cabin schedule. The controller commands the outflow valve to control the amount of air that leaves the cabin. When the valve closes, the cabin pressure increases. When the valve opens, the cabin pressure decreases.

The controller normally changes the cabin pressure slowly during climb and descent. This pressure change helps passengers equalize pressure in the middle ear. The controller also limits the cabin altitude during cruise. If one controller fails, another controller can control the outflow valve on many aircraft.

Safety devices protect the cabin from excessive pressure. Positive pressure relief valves open when the pressure difference becomes too high. Negative pressure relief valves open when outside pressure becomes higher than cabin pressure. These valves prevent damage to the fuselage and other cabin parts. A dump function can open the outflow valve when the crew needs rapid pressure release.

If the system cannot keep a safe pressure, oxygen masks drop from their storage units. The masks supply oxygen while the crew starts a descent to a lower altitude. The crew uses the aircraft procedures to identify the fault and control the descent. Doors, windows, and seals must remain correctly installed for the system to work. A warning system alerts the crew when the cabin altitude becomes too high.

task: Explain why aircraft cabins are pressurized and how the system works.
text:
Aircraft cabins are pressurized because the air outside gets dangerously thin as an airliner climbs. At cruising altitude, around 35,000 feet, atmospheric pressure is only a small fraction of what it is at sea level. There isn't enough oxygen pressure for the lungs to move oxygen into the bloodstream efficiently, even though the air is still about 21 percent oxygen. A person exposed to that air without protection would become confused, lose useful consciousness, and eventually die.

The cabin isn't kept at sea-level pressure, though. That would put unnecessary stress on the fuselage and make the aircraft heavier.
