Instead, most airliners maintain a cabin altitude somewhere between roughly 6,000 and 8,000 feet while the plane may be flying twice or three times higher. You can feel the difference: ears pop during climb and descent because the pressure around the eardrum is changing.

Here’s the basic arrangement. Air is taken from the engines, or supplied by electrically driven compressors on some newer aircraft. It is compressed as part of the system, then passes through cooling equipment and air-conditioning packs, because compression makes it extremely hot. Some aircraft mix this fresh, conditioned air with a portion of recirculated cabin air, which has gone through high-efficiency filters. The mixture then enters the cabin through vents, often near the ceiling.

The crucial part is the outflow valve. Fresh air is continuously coming in, but the valve controls how much air leaves the cabin, usually through ducts near the rear of the aircraft. A flight-control system adjusts the valve according to cabin pressure, aircraft altitude, and the planned rate of climb or descent. When the valve closes more, pressure rises. When it opens, pressure falls. It sounds simple, but the control system makes small, constant corrections so passengers don't feel every change.

The fuselage itself acts like a sealed pressure vessel, though not a perfectly sealed one. Windows, doors, seals, and joints are designed to withstand repeated pressure cycles, since every flight effectively inflates and deflates the cabin a little. That repetition is one reason aircraft are inspected so carefully for cracks and metal fatigue.

If pressurization fails, oxygen masks drop from the ceiling. They don't fill the cabin; they give passengers enough oxygen to stay conscious while the pilots descend rapidly to an altitude where normal breathing is safe.

task: Explain how error-correcting codes recover corrupted data.
text:
Error-correcting codes recover corrupted data by adding carefully designed redundancy before information is transmitted or stored. Instead of sending only the original message, an encoding algorithm calculates extra symbols, called parity symbols or check symbols, and attaches them to the data. These additional symbols do not usually contain new information, but they create mathematical relationships that allow a decoder to detect and sometimes repair errors.

For example, a simple code might represent each bit three times: 0 becomes 000 and 1 becomes 111. If the receiver gets 101, it can use majority voting to infer that the intended value was 111, correcting the middle error. This approach is easy to understand but inefficient, because it requires three times as many bits and cannot reliably correct multiple errors.

More advanced codes use algebraic structures to provide stronger protection with less redundancy. In a block code, a message is divided into fixed-size blocks, and each block is transformed into a longer codeword. The added check symbols give the codeword a particular mathematical structure. When a codeword arrives, the decoder calculates its “syndrome,” a set of values that indicates whether the received pattern is valid and, if not, provides clues about the location and nature of errors.

Some codes can correct errors directly, while others can only detect them. If the number of corrupted symbols is within the code’s correction capacity, the decoder identifies the most likely original codeword. This is often done by comparing the received sequence with valid codewords and choosing the one with the smallest difference, measured by Hamming distance. If too many errors occur, the decoder may report failure rather than risk silently producing incorrect data.

Error-correcting codes are used in many settings. Compact discs and QR codes use them to remain readable despite scratches, dirt, or missing sections. Wireless networks and satellites use them to compensate for interference and weak signals. Computer memory and storage systems use them to detect and repair bit flips caused by electrical noise, aging hardware, or radiation.

The key trade-off is redundancy versus efficiency. More check symbols generally permit more errors to be corrected, but they increase transmission time, storage requirements, and processing work. Well-designed codes balance these costs, enabling reliable communication even when the underlying channel is imperfect.

task: Explain how error-correcting codes recover corrupted data.
text:
An error-correcting code adds extra information to the original data. This extra information is called redundancy. The encoder calculates parity symbols from the data symbols. The encoder sends the data symbols and parity symbols as one codeword.

Noise can change bits or symbols during storage or transmission. A changed value is an error. The receiver gets the codeword, but it does not know which values changed. The decoder calculates new parity results from the received values. The decoder compares these results with the received parity symbols. A difference creates a syndrome.

The syndrome shows the error location or the error pattern. For a single-bit error, a Hamming code can identify the incorrect bit. The decoder changes that bit to its other value. The decoder then checks the corrected codeword again. If all parity checks agree, the decoder sends the recovered data to the application.

Some codes use symbols larger than one bit. A Reed-Solomon code can protect groups of bits as mathematical symbols. This code can correct several changed symbols in a data block. It can also correct erased symbols when their locations are known. An erased symbol can result from a missing storage block or a damaged transmission packet.

The code strength depends on the minimum distance between valid codewords. A code with distance three can correct one error. The same code can detect two errors. In general, a code with distance \(d\) can detect \(d-1\) errors. It can correct up to the integer value of \((d-1)/2\) errors.

The encoder must select enough parity symbols for the expected error level. More parity symbols improve correction strength, but they also increase the codeword size. The receiver can then use the extra symbols to test possible data values. If the error count stays within the code limit, the decoder recovers the original data.

If too many errors occur, the decoder can report a correction failure. Some codes can detect this condition with an additional check value. A cyclic redundancy check can detect many error patterns, but it normally cannot correct them. The system can request the damaged data again when a return path is available. A system without a return path can discard the block or use a backup copy. Interleaving can spread a burst error across several codewords. Each codeword can then correct a smaller number of errors.

task: Explain how error-correcting codes recover corrupted data.
text:
When data travels through a noisy channel, some bits can change. A zero might arrive as a one. A burst of interference could damage several neighboring bits at once. If the receiver has no extra information, it can’t tell whether the received message is original or corrupted.

Error-correcting codes solve that problem by adding carefully calculated redundancy to the data. The extra bits aren’t copies of the whole message. They’re more like clues about what the message is supposed to look like.

Take a simple example. Suppose a sender wants to transmit three bits: `101`. Instead of sending only those bits, it might use a repetition code and send each bit three times: `111000111` for `101`. If the receiver gets `111001111`, it can inspect each group of three. The middle group is `001`, which most likely represents zero because two of its three bits are zero. That’s crude, and it wastes a lot of space, but it shows the basic idea: agreement among redundant information lets the receiver repair an error.

Real systems use smarter codes. In a parity-check code, extra bits are calculated from groups of data bits. For instance, one parity bit might be set so that a particular group always contains an even number of ones. At the receiving end, the system checks those rules. The pattern of failed checks, called a syndrome, helps identify where an error occurred. Once the location is known, the bad bit can be flipped.

Some codes, such as Reed-Solomon codes, work with chunks of symbols rather than individual bits. They’re especially good at handling bursts of damage, which is why they’ve been used on CDs, DVDs, QR codes, and data sent over imperfect connections. A scratched disc might lose a run of bytes, but the mathematical structure added during encoding can reconstruct them.

There’s a limit, though. If too much data is damaged, the code may be unable to decide what the original was. Error correction works only when the corruption stays within the code’s designed tolerance. Systems often report this as a correction capability: a code may fix up to a certain number of errors, or detect more errors than it can repair.

The clever part is that the sender does the extra work before transmission, while the receiver uses the resulting patterns to separate likely truth from random damage. No pristine channel required. Just enough redundancy, and some math.

task: Argue whether universities should ban laptops in lecture halls.
text:
Universities should not impose a blanket ban on laptops in lecture halls, although they should regulate their use. A laptop can be an important academic tool, allowing students to take detailed notes, access readings, search unfamiliar terms, and use specialised software during class. For students with disabilities, typing may be significantly easier than handwriting, and some learners rely on screen readers, enlarged text, or other assistive technologies. An absolute prohibition could therefore reduce accessibility and unfairly disadvantage students whose needs are not immediately visible.

Laptops can also support a more active form of learning. Instructors may ask students to analyse data, consult digital sources, complete online quizzes, or collaborate on shared documents. These activities are increasingly common in higher education and cannot always be performed effectively with pen and paper. Furthermore, university students are adults who should gradually learn to manage distractions and make responsible decisions about their own study habits. Treating them as incapable of exercising judgement may be both patronising and educationally counterproductive.

Nevertheless, the objections to unrestricted laptop use are substantial. Students who browse social media, watch videos, or shop online are less likely to understand a lecture, even if they believe they are multitasking successfully. Their behaviour can distract people sitting nearby, while the sound and movement of constant typing may disrupt the atmosphere of a class. Research also suggests that handwriting can encourage students to process and summarise ideas rather than transcribe every word mechanically. In addition, open laptops can make it harder for lecturers to create eye contact and discussion, weakening the social dimension of teaching.

A better policy would distinguish between harmful and legitimate use. Universities could ask students to keep laptops closed during particular discussions, demonstrations, or examinations, while permitting them for note-taking and approved activities. Lecturers might designate laptop-free sections for students who prefer fewer distractions and provide digital materials beforehand. Clear expectations, occasional monitoring, and reasonable consequences for disruptive use would address the main problems without removing valuable technology from everyone.

Thus, universities should manage laptops rather than ban them. Flexible rules can protect concentration and classroom interaction while preserving accessibility, practical learning, and student autonomy. The goal should be better teaching, not a simplistic attachment to either paper or screens.

task: Argue whether universities should ban laptops in lecture halls.
text:
Universities should ban personal laptops in most lecture halls. The main reason is simple: laptops can divide attention during a lecture. A student can read messages, visit websites, or watch videos instead of giving attention to the lecturer. This activity can distract nearby students, even when the screen stays quiet. A clear rule can help students give the lecturer their full attention.

Laptop use also changes the way students record information. Many students copy each sentence and do not decide which ideas matter. This method can produce long notes, but it can reduce thought and memory. Handwritten notes usually require students to select, shorten, and organize information. That mental work can help students understand the subject during the lecture.

A ban can also improve contact between students and lecturers. Students can look at the speaker, ask questions, and join a discussion. The lecturer can see confusion more easily when screens do not hide faces. The lecture hall can then become a place for active exchange, not only a place for information transfer. This change can support better questions and clearer answers.

A complete ban, however, can create serious problems for some students. Some students need a laptop because of a disability, a medical condition, or a special educational need. Others may need a computer for a technical task, a calculation, or a course exercise. Universities should provide an exception process before they apply a ban. Lecturers should also provide printed notes or digital files for students with approved exceptions.

The rule should also include a short laptop period when a task needs computer access. For example, a lecturer can start a software demonstration and give a clear time limit. Students can then close their laptops before the lecture continues. The university should explain the rule, train lecturers, and apply it in every similar lecture. For these reasons, universities should ban laptops in ordinary lectures, but permit reasonable exceptions. The policy should focus on attention, not punishment, and lecturers should give a reminder before they report repeated wrong use.

task: Argue whether universities should ban laptops in lecture halls.
text:
Universities shouldn’t ban laptops in lecture halls, but they should stop pretending that every student uses them responsibly.

A laptop can be a genuinely useful academic tool. Students can search up an unfamiliar term, pull up the assigned reading, organize notes, or check a diagram that the lecturer has mentioned but not displayed. For students with disabilities, typing may be far easier than handwriting. Some people simply think better when they can write quickly and structure their notes as the lecture moves along. A total ban would treat all of those students as distractions waiting to happen.

Still, the case against laptops is stronger than many universities admit. In a large lecture, one person watching a football clip or scrolling through messages can distract an entire row. Even students who aren’t looking at the screen may start wondering what’s happening on it. And research on note-taking has often found that students remember less when they type everything word for word, since transcription can replace actual processing. I’ve sat in lectures where half the room was apparently taking notes, yet the glow of dozens of screens made the place feel more like an airport lounge than a classroom.

The answer shouldn’t be a blanket ban. It should be a clear policy shaped by the course. In a philosophy or history lecture, where students need to follow an argument, handwritten notes might be encouraged. In computer science, engineering, or a class built around data analysis, banning laptops would be absurd. Professors should be allowed to set reasonable rules, including laptop-free sessions when they can explain why the restriction helps.

Universities could also create laptop-free sections rather than forcing everyone into one system. Students who prefer paper could choose those rooms, while others could sit in regular sections. Phones are a different problem, though. They’re harder to justify during most lectures because they invite constant interruptions and offer little advantage that a laptop doesn’t provide.

A ban sounds satisfyingly simple, which is probably why administrators like it. But classrooms aren’t factories, and students aren’t interchangeable. The better policy is limited laptop use, backed by consequences for obvious misuse, with exceptions for accessibility and course requirements. That asks students to behave like adults without pretending every glowing screen is an enemy.

task: Argue whether remote work is better for early-career engineers.
text:
Remote work can be better for early-career engineers, but only when it is designed to provide deliberate mentorship, clear communication, and meaningful opportunities to collaborate. Without those supports, an office environment usually offers stronger advantages for people still developing technical and professional judgment.

The main benefit of remote work is that it can accelerate independent problem-solving. Junior engineers often need time to investigate documentation, test hypotheses, and learn how systems fit together. Working remotely can reduce interruptions and allow them to concentrate. It may also expose them to colleagues across locations, giving them access to specialized expertise that a single local office cannot provide. In addition, remote work can improve flexibility, reduce commuting stress, and make engineering careers more accessible to people who live far from technology hubs or have disabilities and family responsibilities.

However, early-career development depends on more than completing assigned tickets. New engineers learn many important skills by observing how experienced colleagues debug incidents, review code, negotiate trade-offs, and communicate uncertainty. In an office, a junior engineer can ask a quick question, overhear a useful technical discussion, or notice how a senior engineer responds to a production problem. Remote communication tends to make these interactions more formal. A new employee may hesitate to schedule a meeting for a small question, remain invisible during video calls, or misunderstand an answer because they lack context. As a result, remote workers can become isolated or receive feedback less frequently.

Remote work is therefore best for early-career engineers when companies compensate for the loss of informal learning. Teams should pair junior engineers with mentors, conduct frequent one-on-one meetings, use collaborative programming and design reviews, document decisions, and create predictable opportunities for casual conversation. Managers must also evaluate remote employees by their results rather than by online visibility, while ensuring that junior staff receive challenging assignments instead of only routine tasks. Occasional in-person gatherings can strengthen relationships without requiring permanent office attendance.

Overall, remote work is not automatically better, but it can be better for early-career engineers in a well-structured organization. A poorly managed remote team may slow growth, whereas a thoughtful hybrid or remote-first team can combine focused work, broad access to expertise, and intentional mentorship. The decisive factor is not location; it is whether the workplace makes learning visible, frequent, and accessible.

task: Argue whether remote work is better for early-career engineers.
text:
Remote work can be better for early-career engineers when the company gives strong support. It removes daily travel and gives workers more control of their time. This control can help new engineers study tools, prepare questions, and complete difficult tasks. It can also give access to jobs that are far from a worker's home.

But early-career engineers need frequent contact with experienced people. In an office, a new engineer can ask a short question and receive an immediate answer. The new engineer can also observe design reviews, fault checks, and other work. Remote work can reduce these useful chances if the team uses only written messages.

Remote work also creates a risk of weak professional ties. A new engineer may hesitate to request help during a video meeting. A manager may not notice confusion when the engineer stays quiet. Without regular feedback, small errors can remain until they become costly problems. For this reason, remote teams must set clear meeting times and response rules.

A good remote program can reduce these risks. Each new engineer should have a named mentor and a regular private meeting. The mentor can review work, explain decisions, and give direct feedback. The team should also use video calls for design work and short questions. Written records can help new engineers review instructions after each meeting.

Office work has clear benefits, but it also has limits. A noisy office can interrupt work, and some new engineers may avoid questions in a busy room. Remote work can provide a calmer place and fair access to experts. The best choice depends on the team, the task, and the worker's needs.

For most early-career engineers, a mixed model is better than a fully remote model. The worker can spend planned days with the team and complete focused tasks at home. The company must measure skill growth and work quality, not only time online. With good mentorship, clear communication, and regular office contact, remote work can support a strong start. Without that structure, office work is usually the safer choice.

task: Argue whether remote work is better for early-career engineers.
text:
Remote work is better for some early-career engineers, but as a default, I think the office still has an edge.

That may sound old-fashioned. It isn’t. Junior engineers learn a huge amount by accident: overhearing a staff engineer explain a design choice, seeing how a bug gets investigated, noticing that someone tests an assumption before writing three hundred lines of code. Those moments rarely appear on a calendar. In a remote job, learning is often reduced to scheduled meetings and messages that begin with, “Sorry to bother you.” A new engineer can spend half a day stuck because they don’t know who to ask, or because asking feels like an interruption.

The office makes some of that friction disappear. You can turn around and say, “Can you look at this?” You pick up vocabulary, habits, and context without having to request a formal lesson. That matters early on, when you don’t yet know which questions are smart, which tools are standard, or how much uncertainty is normal.

Still, remote work has real advantages, and they aren’t minor. A quiet home setup can be far better for concentrating than an open office full of conversations and pings. Remote teams also force companies to document decisions, write clearer tickets, and communicate deliberately. Those are excellent engineering habits. Some junior developers thrive remotely because they’re independent, organized, and comfortable asking precise questions in writing. They may produce better work than they would in a noisy office where senior colleagues are constantly interrupting them.

But “remote” only works well when the team has built a strong system around it. Junior engineers need frequent one-on-ones, patient code reviews, easy access to mentors, and an onboarding process that explains more than where the repository lives. If the company simply hands a new hire a laptop and a vague task, remote work becomes isolation with a salary.

The best arrangement is probably hybrid, though not the lazy version where everyone comes in for meaningless meetings. Early-career engineers should have regular in-person time with the people who review their code and make technical decisions. The rest of the week can be remote, giving them room to focus.

So yes, remote work can be better. But for most beginners, a completely remote role is a gamble. I’d choose a supportive hybrid team over a prestigious remote job every time.

task: Argue whether public transit should be fare-free.
text:
Public transit should become fare-free, at least on local buses and trains funded by cities and regional governments. Eliminating fares would not solve every transportation problem, but it would make mobility more equitable, improve access to opportunity, and produce benefits that extend beyond individual riders.

The strongest argument is economic. For low-income workers, students, older adults, and people with disabilities, daily fares can consume a significant share of a limited budget. A person who must take two buses to work may pay more than someone who can drive a car, even though the rider has fewer resources. Fare-free transit would reduce this burden and make it easier for people to reach jobs, schools, medical appointments, and grocery stores. It would also remove the humiliation and inconvenience that occur when passengers cannot afford a fare or lack the correct payment method.

Free service could improve public transportation in other ways. Fare collection requires machines, enforcement officers, payment systems, and administrative work. Those resources could instead support more frequent service, cleaner vehicles, safer stations, and expanded routes. Boarding would be faster when passengers do not have to search for money or tap a card, potentially making buses more reliable. In addition, fare-free transit could encourage some drivers to leave their cars at home, reducing traffic congestion, air pollution, and greenhouse-gas emissions.

However, eliminating fares is not costless. Transit agencies depend on fare revenue, and replacing it would require reliable public funding. If governments fail to provide enough money, free transit could mean overcrowded vehicles and less frequent service. Moreover, some riders who can afford fares might receive a benefit they do not need, while taxpayers who rarely use transit would help pay for it. Critics also argue that fares can discourage disorderly behavior, although enforcement policies—not prices alone—are more directly responsible for safety.

These concerns suggest that fare-free transit must be paired with dedicated funding, careful planning, and strong service standards. Governments could finance it through progressive taxes, congestion charges, or fees on large employers that benefit from accessible transportation. If universal fare-free service is not immediately feasible, cities should begin with free transit for children, low-income residents, and routes connecting underserved neighborhoods.

Ultimately, public transit is not merely a product purchased by individual passengers; it is public infrastructure that benefits entire communities. With adequate investment, fare-free transit would be a practical and fair step toward a healthier, more accessible city.

task: Argue whether public transit should be fare-free.
text:
Public transit should become fare-free in many cities. This policy lets each person travel without a payment at a bus or train entrance. The policy can improve access to work, school, health care, and public services. It can also reduce traffic on busy roads.

A fare can stop a person from making an important trip. A low-income worker can lose a job after a small change in travel cost. A student can miss a class when the student has no money for a ticket. Fare-free transit removes this direct barrier and gives people more choice. This result supports equal access to the city.

Fare-free transit can also make the transit system faster. Passengers do not wait for a ticket machine or a fare check. Drivers can focus on the road instead of fare collection. The city can remove some machines and reduce their repair cost. These changes can shorten stops and improve service on busy routes.

More passengers may leave cars at home when transit has no fare. Fewer cars can reduce traffic, fuel use, noise, and air pollution. Cleaner air can support public health, especially near large roads. A city can also use less road space for car travel.

Fare-free transit does not solve every transit problem. A free trip can increase demand before the city adds buses, trains, and staff. Crowded vehicles can reduce comfort and can make service less reliable. The city must improve routes, schedules, safety, and vehicle condition at the same time.

The largest concern is the loss of fare revenue. The city must replace this money with taxes, grants, or other public funds. Officials must show the cost of the policy before they start it. They must also report service quality and passenger numbers at regular times. Clear reports can help the public judge the result.

Some cities may not have enough funds for a complete fare-free system. They can start with free transit for children, older people, or low-income passengers. They can also make selected routes free during peak traffic periods. These trials can provide useful data before a larger decision.

A city should not call transit fare-free and then reduce service. The city should set a clear service standard and protect the required funds. It should measure access, travel time, traffic, pollution, and passenger safety. If the city can meet these conditions, fare-free transit is a strong public choice. It gives more people access while it supports cleaner and safer streets.

task: Argue whether public transit should be fare-free.
text:
Public transit should be fare-free, at least on buses and local trains within cities. The argument isn’t that transportation costs nothing. Someone still pays for drivers, fuel, repairs, and new vehicles. The question is whether that money should come from the fare box or from the broader public budget. In most cases, public funding makes more sense.

Fares create a small wall around the city. For people with steady incomes, a couple of dollars may seem trivial. For someone working part-time, missing a paycheck, or raising children alone, those dollars add up quickly. A person might skip a doctor’s appointment, turn down a job across town, or risk walking home at night because the fare is sitting between them and the bus. That’s a bad system.

Fare-free transit would also speed up boarding. Drivers wouldn’t have to wait while passengers search for change or argue with a malfunctioning card reader. The savings from eliminating fare collection wouldn’t cover the whole cost of transit, but they’d offset part of it. More riders would likely use the system, too, especially for short trips that people currently make by car.

And fewer car trips matter. Transportation is one of the biggest sources of urban pollution, while traffic wastes enormous amounts of time and space. If buses are free but slow, unreliable, and stuck behind cars, people won’t abandon their vehicles in large numbers. Fare-free service isn’t a magic switch. It has to come with frequent routes, clean vehicles, safe stops, and priority lanes that keep buses moving.

There are legitimate concerns. Free service can attract disruptive behavior, and crowded buses may become even more crowded. Transit agencies could lose revenue if governments promise free rides and then underfund the system. That would be worse than charging a modest fare. A broken “free” network is not a public benefit.

Still, the answer is to fund transit properly, not to preserve a barrier that falls hardest on people with the least money. Cities already pay for roads, parking enforcement, and traffic management whether every resident drives or not. Transit deserves the same treatment. It’s public infrastructure, like sidewalks and libraries. Nobody demands that a library charge at the door to prove it has value. Public transit should be treated with the same basic confidence.

task: Argue whether high schools should require a computer science credit.
text:
High schools should require students to earn at least one computer science credit before graduation. In a society shaped by algorithms, digital networks, and automation, understanding technology is no longer a specialized skill reserved for future programmers. It is a form of literacy, like reading, mathematics, and scientific reasoning.

A computer science course can teach students how to break complicated problems into manageable steps, recognize patterns, evaluate evidence, and develop solutions through testing and revision. These skills apply far beyond software development. Students may use computational thinking in fields such as medicine, journalism, business, engineering, art, and public service. Even those who never write code will encounter automated decisions, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity threats, and data collection in their personal and professional lives. Learning how programs work can help students use technology responsibly rather than accepting digital systems as mysterious or unquestionable.

A requirement could also improve equity. Students from affluent families may have access to coding camps, personal tutors, or advanced technology programs, while others may not receive any formal exposure to computer science. Making one course available to everyone would ensure that technological knowledge is not limited to students who already have opportunities outside school. It could also encourage underrepresented students to consider careers in a rapidly growing field.

However, schools should implement this requirement thoughtfully. Not every district has enough qualified teachers, updated equipment, or funding. A poorly designed class focused only on memorizing programming commands could frustrate students and fail to provide meaningful learning. Therefore, governments and school systems should support teacher training, provide accessible devices and software, and offer several course options, including introductory programming, cybersecurity, web design, and data science. Computer science should complement rather than replace essential subjects, and students with limited access to technology should receive additional support.

Requiring one computer science credit would not mean turning every student into a programmer. It would give all graduates practical knowledge for navigating a digital world, strengthen problem-solving abilities, and broaden future opportunities. With adequate resources and an inclusive curriculum, the requirement would be a valuable and necessary part of a modern high school education.

task: Argue whether high schools should require a computer science credit.
text:
High schools should require one computer science credit for every student. Computer systems control many parts of modern life, from communication to health care. Students need basic knowledge of data, software, networks, and online safety. A required course can give each student this foundation, not only students who choose advanced classes.

A computer science course can also develop clear thinking. Students can break a large task into small steps and test each step. They can find errors, change a plan, and explain why a solution works. These habits support work in science, mathematics, business, and many other fields.

However, a requirement can create problems if schools lack trained teachers, equipment, or time. Some schools already have full schedules and limited funds. A new course must not remove essential instruction in reading, mathematics, art, or health. School leaders must provide instruction for teachers, suitable devices, and reliable network service before they add the credit.

The requirement must also support students with different needs. Schools must provide accessible software, clear instructions, and extra time when a student needs it. Teachers must not assume that every student has a computer or network service at home. Schools can provide devices, network access, and supervised work time to reduce this gap.

Some people argue that schools should offer computer science as an option. They say students need choice and that a required course can reduce interest. This concern has value, but schools can offer different course levels and practical topics. A beginner course can teach safe Internet use, data privacy, algorithms, and simple program design without requiring advanced mathematics.

For these reasons, high schools should require a basic computer science credit. The course should focus on useful knowledge, careful thought, and responsible technology use. It should not require every student to become a software developer. With proper resources and flexible course design, the requirement can prepare students for work, further education, and daily life.

task: Argue whether high schools should require a computer science credit.
text:
High schools should require at least one computer science credit. Not because every student needs to become a software engineer, but because computers shape nearly every part of adult life, and students deserve to understand more than how to click through an app.

A computer science class teaches students how to break a large problem into smaller pieces, test an idea, find an error, and try again without giving up after the first failure. Those habits matter outside programming. A student balancing a budget, studying biology, or organizing a community project benefits from learning how systems work and how to approach confusing problems logically. Writing code can be frustrating, too, which is partly the point. Students get used to making mistakes they can actually inspect and fix.

There’s a practical reason for the requirement as well. Technology affects jobs in fields that used to seem unrelated to computers. Nurses work with electronic records and data systems. Journalists analyze information and publish through digital platforms. Factory workers operate automated equipment. Even small-business owners have to think about websites, security, and software subscriptions. A basic course could give students enough knowledge to understand what these tools are doing, rather than treating technology as magic supplied by somebody else.

Still, schools shouldn’t pretend that one introductory programming class will prepare everyone for the tech industry. It won’t. And a poorly designed course, built around memorizing commands or rushing through complicated software, could make students hate the subject. The class should include programming, but it should also cover online privacy, algorithms, artificial intelligence, and the way digital systems can reinforce unfair decisions. Students need to question technology, not just use it.

Some people argue that graduation requirements are already crowded. That’s true. But computer science shouldn’t be added by squeezing out art, music, career education, or a strong humanities course. Schools should make room for it by offering flexible options, such as an introductory coding course, data science, robotics, or a class focused on computing and society. Students shouldn’t all have to learn the same programming language.

A computer science credit won’t solve every educational problem. It would, however, give teenagers a clearer view of the systems they already depend on. That seems like a reasonable expectation for high school graduates.
